Title: Willa Cather: Nebraska Pioneer and Author
Content: `text(One)` of Nebraska’s most beloved authors is Willa Cather. In `1883`, when Willa was `text(nine years)` old, she traveled with her family from the Blue Ridge Mountains in Virginia to the American frontier in Webster County, Nebraska. It was a dramatic change for Willa. Later, in a book called My Ántonia, she would write about the experience.

After `text(two years)` of farming, the Cather family moved to the nearby town of Red Cloud. Willa thrived in Red Cloud, exploring the countryside, meeting new people, and developing an appreciation for the arts. Cather graduated from Red Cloud High School and the University of Nebraska. Red Cloud and the country surrounding it made a deep impression on Cather. She used its landscape as a setting in many of her novels and short stories.

Cather is `text(one)` of Nebraska’s most noted novelists, yet when she `text(first)` began college, she wanted to become a doctor. When `text(one)` of the stories Cather wrote for a class got published, she discovered a passion for writing. The remaining time she was in college, Cather used her new-found talent to edit the school magazine and write articles and play reviews for the local paper.

After graduating in `1895`, Cather moved to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where she was offered an editing position for Home Monthly. She wrote many short stories during this time and used them in the magazine. She was also a telegraph operator and theater critic for the Daily Leader.

From `1897` to `1906`, Cather worked as a high school English and Latin teacher. During that time, she continued to write and publish stories. In `1903` Cather published a volume of poetry called April Twilights, and in `1905` she published a collection of short stories called The Troll Garden.

Cather’s writing came to the attention of S.S. McClure, the owner of `text(one)` of the most widely read magazines in the United States. In `1906` Cather moved to New York City and became a writer and editor for McClure’s Magazine. While on an assignment in Boston, she met Sara Orne Jewett, who encouraged her to write about her roots in Nebraska. In `1912` Cather left McClure’s Magazine to write full time.

Cather published her `text(first)` novel, Alexander’s Bridge, in `1912`. `text(One year)` later, she published O Pioneers!—a novel set in the windswept frontier of Nebraska. During that time, she met up with an old friend from Red Cloud named Annie Sadilek. Cather based the main character of her next book, My Ántonia, on her friend. My Ántonia, published in `1918`, was another story about Nebraska. It celebrated the land and the immigrant pioneers, and it is considered `text(one)` of Cather’s finest works.

In `1923` Cather won the Pulitzer Prize for One of Ours, her novel about a Nebraska farm boy who goes off to fight in World War I. She went on to write several more books and win many awards for her writing. Each of her books was met with widespread praise and admiration.

Many of her books drew on her memories and knowledge of Nebraska. Cather has been thought of as a `ultext(chronicler)` of the American pioneer. Her novels express her deep love of the land and exhibit a strong sense of place. She created strong female characters and emphasized the importance of family and the need for human courage and dignity.

Cather was the `text(first)` woman admitted into the Nebraska Hall of Fame. The Willa Cather Pioneer Memorial and Education Foundation is located in Red Cloud, Nebraska. There, her childhood home and other buildings connected to her writings have been preserved. Surrounding the site are `text(210 acres)` of native grassland called the Willa Cather Memorial Prairie. Standing on the prairie, people today can imagine what it was like a `text(hundred years)` before, when Cather wrote, “Elsewhere the sky is the roof of the world; but here the earth was the floor of the sky.”
